candidates.text: James Mulcahy claims to have been at Mancuso’s pool hall at 8:30 PM but cannot say that the challenger went down in the fourth and the crowd booed it, which everybody there can.
The beat cop’s pass at 6:00 PM puts James Mulcahy at the speakeasy under the hat shop.
The beat cop’s pass at 7:30 PM puts Wilhelm Schilling at the stairwell of the Mott Street tenement.
The beat cop’s pass at 10:30 PM puts Nora Corrigan, Sol Sirkin, Konrad Obermann, Wilhelm Schilling, James Mulcahy at Mancuso’s pool hall.
Found at Mancuso’s pool hall: A promissory note for $4,000 signed by Konrad Obermann, endorsed to Klara Kreuzer, three months past due.
Gretchen Hauck says Klara Kreuzer told Konrad Obermann that Friday was the end of it, one way or the other.
Found at the vestibule of the Hallam apartments: A lease assignment made out in James Mulcahy’s name, waiting only on Klara Kreuzer’s signature.
Bella Margolis says Klara Kreuzer told James Mulcahy the lease would go to somebody else at the quarter day.
Maureen Doyle hired us. Maureen Doyle wants it known that Konrad Obermann owed the victim money, and would rather we started there.
Sol Sirkin on Nora Corrigan: Nora Corrigan’s sleeves are buttoned at the wrist in a warm room.
Wilhelm Schilling on Nora Corrigan: Somebody at the subway kiosk at the corner sells what a druggist will not, and Nora Corrigan knows which door.
Gretchen Hauck on Nora Corrigan: Nora Corrigan was steady at nine and shaking at seven, and it was not nerves about the police.
A paper of powder at the subway kiosk at the corner, folded the way one particular hand folds them.
A prescription blank at the subway kiosk at the corner signed by a doctor who has been dead since the spring.
The man who sells it at the subway kiosk at the corner gives it up rather than be held: Nora Corrigan was there from 8:30 PM, and stayed until it took hold.
The doctor Nora Corrigan used to see confirms the habit and the hour: Nora Corrigan was at the subway kiosk at the corner from 8:30 PM, and could not have crossed the street unhelped.
Albrecht Wehrle on Maureen Doyle: Maureen Doyle and the victim were heard at the vestibule of the Hallam apartments, and one of them was doing all the talking.
Nora Corrigan on Maureen Doyle: Maureen Doyle has come into money lately and has no visible way of having come into money.
Konrad Obermann on Maureen Doyle: The victim had been drawing cash in amounts that did not match anything in the accounts.
An envelope at the vestibule of the Hallam apartments with nothing in it, addressed in the victim’s hand to no one.
A photograph at the vestibule of the Hallam apartments, folded small, of something the victim would have paid to keep folded.

The victim’s bank book settles it: four payments, and Maureen Doyle at the vestibule of the Hallam apartments from 7:00 PM to 7:30 PM collecting the fifth. It is extortion, and an extortionist wants the man alive.
The thing Maureen Doyle was holding over the victim turns up, and it was worth more to Maureen Doyle every month than once.
Abraham Abramowitz on Sol Sirkin: Sol Sirkin was carrying a parcel into Mancuso’s pool hall and came out without it.
Bella Margolis on Sol Sirkin: There is a man who meets people at Mancuso’s pool hall and nobody will say his name out loud.
Lyman Bidwell on Sol Sirkin: Sol Sirkin has been selling things that were never Sol Sirkin’s to sell.
Wrapping paper and a cut string at Mancuso’s pool hall, and the shop it came from closed two years ago.
A pawn ticket at Mancuso’s pool hall in a name that does not exist, made out at the hour in question.

The receiver at Mancuso’s pool hall would rather talk than be held: Sol Sirkin was there from 9:00 PM handing over a parcel of somebody else’s silver, which is a charge Sol Sirkin will take over this one.
The goods turn up, tagged and dated, and the tag puts Sol Sirkin at Mancuso’s pool hall from 9:00 PM with both hands full.
